name: Illusory truth effect
statement: Repeating a claim makes people rate it as truer, whether or not it is true and whether or not they already know better.
meaning: Repetition carries no information about whether a claim is correct. The proposal is that hearing it again raises the rating anyway, because a statement encountered before is easier to read and process, and that ease gets read as a signal of truth. The literature measures the effect two ways. The within-items version compares a statement's rating on first encounter with its rating on second encounter. The between-items version compares repeated statements against new ones at the same test. They are not interchangeable. Dechêne and colleagues' 2010 abstract reports the between-items effect as the larger, and the 2026 meta-analysis excluded within-item studies outright, so its pooled figure describes the between-items form only. Liking rather than believing is the mere-exposure effect, entry 21. Inferring size or quantity from how fast something comes to mind is the fluency heuristic, entry 245.

origin.who: Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino
origin.where: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
origin.note: The paper is "Frequency and the Conference of Referential Validity", and it uses the term referential validity rather than illusory truth. The name in current use came later, and the entry keeps 1977 because that is the study the effect is built on.

evidence: Hasher, Goldstein and Toppino ran 50 college students and analysed 40, discarding ten who missed a session. Each heard 60 plausible assertions on three occasions two weeks apart and rated validity on a seven-point scale. The 140-item pool was culled from reference works on ten topics including history, sports, demography and the arts, seven true and seven false per topic, written to be plausible without being known. Twenty items recurred at every session. Mean ratings for the repeated items ran 4.35, 4.67 and 4.74 across the three sessions; for the non-repeated ones they ran 4.25, 4.22 and 4.16. The repetition by session interaction held, F(2, 78) = 11.80, p < .01, with a rise for repeated items, F(2, 78) = 16.34, and no change for the rest, F < 1. Actual truth or falsity entered no interaction, so repetition moved true and false statements alike. At session one the items due to recur and those not did not differ, F(1, 39) = 1.69, p > .05. Later work pushed on the assumption that knowledge blocks the effect. Fazio, Brashier, Payne and Marsh's first experiment gave 40 Duke undergraduates statements drawn from general-knowledge norms and checked afterwards what each participant knew. Repeated falsehoods scored 3.53 against 3.26 for new ones, F(1, 39) = 13.06, p = .001, partial eta-squared = .25, and knowledge did not interact with repetition, F(1, 39) = 1.21, p = .28. For contradictions of facts the participant demonstrably knew, repeated statements still scored 2.93 against 2.59, t(39) = 2.93, p = .006.

replication.headline: A 2026 meta-analysis of 182 studies and 31,184 people put the effect at g = 0.37 after correcting for small-study bias, and a 2026 registered replication found it again.
replication.detail: Ye, Attali, Ghazi, Cachia, Cassotti and Borst pooled 366 effect sizes from 182 studies in 99 articles published between 1977 and 2025, covering 31,184 participants. Studies using the within-item criterion were excluded, so the pooled figure is a between-items estimate. Their funnel plot and Egger test showed asymmetry, t(364) = 9.77, p < .001, so they applied a PEESE correction and used the corrected model as the baseline for everything else. The corrected estimate is g = 0.37, 95% CI [0.30, 0.44], with sensitivity analyses running from g = 0.35, 95% CI [0.29, 0.42] to g = 0.44, 95% CI [0.37, 0.51] depending on how missing standard deviations and correlations were imputed. Heterogeneity is large, Q(364) = 4,445, p < .001. Moderators do most of the interesting work. Asking people to judge truth at first exposure cut the effect to g = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.23], against g = 0.42 when the first-exposure task was unrelated. Marking a statement false at first exposure reversed it to g = -0.18, against g = 0.43 with no cue. News headlines gave g = 0.17 against g = 0.41 for standard statements, t(147) = 2.10, p = .038. That contrast is weaker than the other two, which both ran below p < .001. Single studies point the same way. Bowes and Fazio's registered replication ran 297 American adults from CloudResearch Connect and analysed 296. Repeated statements were rated truer than new ones, F(1, 295) = 29.32, p < .001, partial eta-squared = .09, for conspiracy claims, dz = 0.18, and for plausibility-matched trivia, dz = 0.26. The second study of Fazio, Rand and Pennycook, preregistered, had 503 people complete it on Mechanical Turk and found repeated statements rated true 52% of the time against 48% for novel ones, t(502) = 9.19, p < .001, d = 0.41. The second study of Pennycook, Cannon and Rand used real fake-news headlines and kept 949 of the 1,069 who started. A single prior exposure raised accuracy ratings from 1.65 to 1.77, t(948) = 7.60, p < .001, d = 0.25. Stump, Hartmann and Klauer showed 165 people Instagram-style posts and found the effect again on the odds of a "true" judgment, b = 1.905, p < .001, with visible like counts not moderating it.

study.cite: Ye, S., Attali, D., Ghazi, M., Cachia, A., Cassotti, M., & Borst, G. (2026). Systematic review and meta-analysis of the evidence for an illusory truth effect and its determinants. Nature Communications, 17(1), 3270.

limits: The full text of Dechêne, Stahl, Hansen and Wänke's 2010 meta-analysis could not be obtained for this entry. The publisher's copy is paywalled, Unpaywall records no open location, and PubMed carries only the abstract. Its pooled figures are quoted here at one remove. Ye and colleagues describe it as covering 51 studies and 102 effect sizes published up to 2006, with estimates from d = 0.39, 95% CI [0.32, 0.47] to d = 0.50, 95% CI [0.43, 0.57] depending on whether the model was fixed or random effects and which criterion was used. They attach d = 0.39 to the within-item criterion and d = 0.53 to the between-item one. Dechêne and colleagues' own abstract, which was read, says the between-items effect is the larger. Those numbers have not been checked against the full paper. No multi-lab test of the effect was located. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, OSF preprints and the open web for multi-lab, multi-site and Psychological Science Accelerator work on the illusory truth effect returned none, and the 2026 meta-analysis cites none. Henderson, Westwood and Simons searched 16 bibliographic and grey literature databases and mapped 93 reports and 181 studies. All were conducted at Western universities, in 12 countries. With external replications, preregistrations, data and code lacking, they write, replicability and robustness can be verified for only a small number of studies. They name Accelerator-style multi-lab work as the way to close the gap. The effect decays. Henderson, Simons and Barr ran a registered report against a planned 608 participants, recruited 631 at the first phase and analysed 567, varying the gap between exposure and test. Repeated statements beat new ones at every interval. The gap on their seven-point scale fell from 0.68 immediately to 0.39 after a day, 0.27 after a week and 0.14 after a month, chi-squared(3) = 121.15, p < .001 for the interaction with interval. Campaign material has not reproduced the effect. Dash, Xu, Jalbert and Spiro showed 1,200 Americans verbatim or machine-paraphrased posts drawn from two United States disinformation campaigns. Neither raised belief in the exact claim, a related claim or the broad narrative against a control. The two comparisons nearest the line are ones the authors themselves call marginal: b = 0.133, 95% CI [-0.021, 0.287], P = 0.091 for the paraphrased exact claim, and b = 0.129, 95% CI [0.000, 0.259], P = 0.051 for the verbatim related claim. Perceived consensus did move. Fazio's 2020 Collabra paper is open access, but its full text could not be retrieved through the publisher, DOAJ or Europe PMC, so this entry rests on its published abstract alone. Lacassagne and colleagues' figures below come from the authors' submitted manuscript on OSF; the published Cognition article is paywalled and was not read. The pooled g of 0.37 is small, it is an average over conditions that differ by a factor of four, and the corpus it comes from shows clear small-study effects before correction. Almost all of the evidence is ratings on a scale, not decisions or behaviour.
misreadings: The popular form of the claim is that repeating a lie often enough turns it into a believed truth. What the studies show is a shift in average rating, usually a fraction of a point on a six- or seven-point scale, not the conversion of disbelief into belief. Repetition is also often described as working only on claims people have no view about. That condition belongs to the later literature rather than to Hasher and colleagues, who wrote about plausible statements and found actual truth or falsity made no difference to the result. Dechêne and colleagues stated it in 2010, Fazio, Brashier, Payne and Marsh tested and rejected it in 2015, and Fazio ran the test again in 2020 with prior knowledge measured before the manipulation rather than after. The opposite overstatement circulates too. The first study of Pennycook, Cannon and Rand found that patently false statements did not budge, 1.13 repeated against 1.11 new, t(408) = 0.74, p = .462, and that reads as a floor on the effect. Fazio, Rand and Pennycook then showed by simulation that a constant repetition effect produces exactly that flat tail through the psychometrics of a binary task. No mechanism that switches off is needed. Lacassagne, Béna and Corneille then repeated blatantly false statements five times and measured truth on a 100-point scale, analysing 232 of 240 Prolific participants. Repeated statements scored 8.79 against 6.43, t(231) = -4.49, d = 0.28, and every judgment stayed far below the scale midpoint. Only 52.58% of the sample showed a positive effect; 19.4% showed none and 28.02% showed a reversal. Warnings are the practical case people get wrong. Tagging a headline "Disputed by 3rd Party Fact-Checkers" at first exposure did not stop the repetition effect, t(447) = 3.07, p = .002, d = 0.14. The meta-analysis separates two things a warning can be. A general warning that some statements are false moved nothing, at exposure or at test. A cue attached to the statement itself and marking it false reversed the effect to g = -0.18, though the subset of those cues that were labels rather than feedback or qualifiers did not, g = 0.04 on five effect sizes. Correcting a claim after it has been believed is a different problem again, and belongs to the continued influence effect, entry 192. Offering repetition in place of an argument is proof by assertion, entry 514.
